note.question: How can markov chain–based policies support multistage stochastic integer linear programming with an application to disaster relief logistics?
note.overview: Multistage stochastic programs involving mixed-integer state variables and continuous local variables (MSILPs) present a challenging class of optimization problems with limited techniques available to obtain high-quality solutions efficiently. These problems arise in many practical applications, including disaster relief logistics planning for natural disasters such as hurricanes, which is increasingly important due to its significant societal impacts. We introduce an aggregation framework to address MSILPs that impose additional structure on the integer state variables by leveraging information from the underlying stochastic process, which is modeled as a Markov chain (MC).

models.summary: Multistage stochastic programs involving mixed-integer state variables and continuous local variables (MSILPs) present a challenging class of optimization problems with limited techniques available to obtain high-quality solutions efficiently. These problems arise in many practical applications, including disaster relief logistics planning for natural disasters such as hurricanes, which is increasingly important due to its significant societal impacts. We demonstrate that the aggregated MSILP can be solved exactly via a branch-and-cut algorithm integrated with a variant of the stochastic dual dynamic programming method.

conditions: We propose a reformulation of (P) as a partially extended formulation, where all integer decisions are treated as first-stage variables.

First, by eliminating integer variables from downstream nodes, the cost-to-go functions at each node n ∈N ∖ {r} become piecewise linear convex and involve only continuous variables, thereby enabling the use of standard Benders-type cutting-plane methods.

More specifically, the key distinction between (PR) and the original formulation (P) is that all integer state variables z = {zn}n∈N , along with Constraints (2a), are now “moved” to the root node problem (i.e., they are treated as first-stage variables and constraints).

conditions: The idea behind 2SLDRs is to replace the continuous state variables xn with new variables at each node n ∈ N via a linear relation based on node-specific data.
Let ξt denote the vector of random variables at stage t ∈[T], and let ξt,n be its realization at node n ∈N t (i.e., ξt,n = {An,Bn,Cn,Dn,En,Fn,Jn,bn,cn,dn,fn,hn}).

Specifically, 2SLDRs employ basis functions Ψt(·) to map ξt n into feature values, which are then used to linearly represent the state variables as xn = μ⊤ t Ψt(ξt n) ∈Rk, where μt is a vector of the LDR variables at stage t.
